extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers in political science (administrative law, bureaucracy)
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and explain McCubbins, Noll, and Weingast's argument that administrative procedures (APAs) function as instruments for elected politicians to control bureaucratic policymaking by changing information flows, enforcement costs, and agency incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis: administrative law as a tool for political control
rubrics_metrics.description: "Specifically, the hypothesis we put forth is that much of administrative law ... is written for the purpose of helping elected politicians retain control of policymaking." (246)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central claim of the article: administrative procedures are designed not only for neutral decisionmaking but to help elected officials keep bureaucratic decisions aligned with political principals' interests. Use this as the baseline evaluative lens when assessing APAs' design and effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: APAs overcome information asymmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: APAs (Administrative Procedures Acts) help overcome information asymmetry. They enable politicians (in executive and legislative branches) to keep administrative decisions in line with their (and their constituents') interests without having to really pay much attention to the bureaucracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted support: "By requiring agencies to collect and disseminate politically relevant information, Congress and the president make the threat of sanctions a more efficacious control device." Evaluate procedures by how much they increase the flow of politically relevant information from agencies to principals and third parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedures increase efficacy of sanctions by producing relevant information
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring agencies to collect and disseminate politically relevant information makes the threat of sanctions a more efficacious control device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess APAs for mechanisms that reveal agency behavior (notice-and-comment, reporting, transparency rules). The more discoverable and salient agency actions are to principals and enforcement actors, the more practical sanctions become.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement cost-shifting to constituents and courts
rubrics_metrics.description: "Moreover, the administrative system is designed so that some of the costs of enforcement are borne not by politicians, but by constituents and the courts."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat as a criterion whether procedures channel enforcement burdens onto outside actors (interest groups, citizens, litigants, courts) rather than requiring costly direct monitoring by elected officials. Consider how procedures enable third-party monitoring and legal challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedures alter agencies' implementation costs and incentives via enfranchisement of opposed groups
rubrics_metrics.description: "Administrative procedures affect the costs to agencies of implementing policies that are opposed by groups enfranchised by these procedures. This alters the incentive structure of the agencies and thereby shapes their decisions."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how procedural participation rights (commenting, hearings, petitioning) change the political and administrative costs of implementing certain policies, thereby influencing agency behavior. Look for how enfranchisement of groups through procedure creates deterrents or bargaining pressures on agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural oversight substitutes for costly direct monitoring ('police patrols')
rubrics_metrics.description: The literature mostly looks to active oversight (i.e. 'police patrols,' monitoring and sanctions) for evidence of political control of the bureaucracy. However, the high cost of monitoring prevents this from working as well as politicians would like; thus APAs are alternative means of control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the relative cost of direct oversight as a criterion: where direct monitoring is too expensive, assess whether procedural rules serve as a low-cost substitute to achieve principals' control objectives. Consider cost-benefit tradeoffs between police-patrol oversight and procedural mechanisms.
